## Proof

**Key observation.** Combine the two real series into one complex series. Define
$$F_N(x) := c_N(x) + i\,s_N(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N}\frac{\cos n + i\sin n}{n!}\,x^n = \sum_{n=0}^{N}\frac{e^{in}}{n!}\,x^n = \sum_{n=0}^{N}\frac{(e^{i}\,x)^n}{n!}.$$

**Convergence.** For every fixed real $x$, the complex number $e^{i}x$ has modulus $|x|$, and the exponential series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{n!}$ converges absolutely for all $z\in\mathbb{C}$ (with value $e^{z}$). Hence, as $N\to\infty$,
$$F_N(x) \longrightarrow F(x) := \exp\!\big(e^{i}\,x\big).$$

**Relating $Q$ to $F_N$.** Since $c_N$ and $s_N$ are real,
$$Q(x,N) = \sqrt{c_N(x)^2 + s_N(x)^2} = \big|c_N(x) + i\,s_N(x)\big| = |F_N(x)|.$$

The modulus is continuous, so
$$\lim_{N\to\infty} Q(x,N) = \lim_{N\to\infty}|F_N(x)| = |F(x)| = \big|\exp(e^{i}x)\big|.$$

**Evaluating the modulus.** Write $e^{i} = \cos 1 + i\sin 1$, so $\operatorname{Re}(e^{i}) = \cos 1$. For real $x$,
$$\exp(e^{i}x) = \exp\!\big((\cos 1)\,x + i(\sin 1)\,x\big) = e^{(\cos 1)x}\cdot e^{i(\sin 1)x},$$
and therefore
$$\big|\exp(e^{i}x)\big| = e^{(\cos 1)x}\cdot\big|e^{i(\sin 1)x}\big| = e^{(\cos 1)x}\cdot 1 = e^{(\cos 1)x}.$$

**Conclusion.** The limit exists for every real $x$, and
$$\boxed{\lim_{N\to\infty} Q(x,N) = e^{(\cos 1)\,x}.}$$

Thus the suspected form $e^{qx}$ is correct with
$$q = \cos 1 \approx 0.5403023058681398\ldots,$$
which indeed satisfies $0.5403 < q < 0.5404$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
